triage.reason: Bleeding with prolonged PT in a newborn or malabsorbing adult; diagnosis reachable from bleeding history, exam and coagulation labs.

age.peak: bimodal: newborns (first days to 12 weeks) and older adults with malabsorption or biliary disease

demographics: Classic early form occurs in breastfed newborns who did not receive vitamin K prophylaxis at birth
Late form (2–12 weeks) occurs almost exclusively in exclusively breastfed infants, often with underlying cholestasis or malabsorption
In adults it occurs in chronic malabsorption, biliary obstruction, prolonged antibiotic use, or severe liver disease

risk_factors.text: Newborn not given vitamin K prophylaxis at birth
Cholestatic liver disease or biliary obstruction
Chronic malabsorption (celiac disease, cystic fibrosis, short bowel, inflammatory bowel disease)
Severe liver disease with impaired synthesis of vitamin K–dependent factors
Warfarin or other vitamin K antagonist therapy
Poor dietary intake of vitamin K (leafy greens) with fat malabsorption

social_history: Strict vegetarian or limited diet without leafy greens (adults)

chief_complaints.text: My baby is bleeding from the umbilical stump
My baby has blood in the diaper
My baby has bruises all over
I am bleeding from my gums and nose
I bruise very easily and bleed a long time from small cuts

hpi.onset: Newborns: bleeding in the first week of life (early) or at 2–12 weeks (late). Adults: gradual over days to weeks as deficiency develops.
hpi.duration: Hours to days of active bleeding; underlying deficiency may have been present for weeks
hpi.progression: Starts with minor oozing from the umbilical stump, circumcision site, or venipuncture sites, then progresses to GI bleeding, extensive bruising, or intracranial hemorrhage if untreated
hpi.location: Skin, mucous membranes, gastrointestinal tract, umbilical stump, circumcision site, or intracranial
hpi.quality: Oozing from puncture sites and mucous membranes; large spreading ecchymoses; blood in stool or vomit
hpi.severity: Variable; can be mild oozing or life-threatening intracranial hemorrhage
hpi.timing: Continuous or recurrent bleeding; new bruises appear without trauma

associated_symptoms.text: Seizures or altered mental status if intracranial bleed

argues_against: Hemophilia pattern of joint and muscle bleeds

atypical.how_it_differs: Late vitamin K deficiency bleeding (2–12 weeks) occurs almost exclusively in exclusively breastfed infants, often with cholestasis; it can present with intracranial hemorrhage and no external bleeding.
Adults with cirrhosis may have prolonged PT from both vitamin K deficiency and impaired synthesis of clotting factors; bleeding may be less responsive to vitamin K alone.
Often presents with GI bleeding or bruising on warfarin or after prolonged antibiotics, rather than umbilical or circumcision bleeding.

general.mild: Well-appearing, active, feeding normally; minor oozing or a few bruises noted
general.moderate: Mildly irritable or fussy; visible bruising or active oozing from a site
general.severe: Lethargic or inconsolable, pale, actively bleeding from mucous membranes or GI tract
general.critical: Shocky, pale or mottled, poorly responsive, signs of intracranial hemorrhage or exsanguinating bleeding

labs.caveat: Prolonged PT is the hallmark; it corrects within hours after vitamin K in simple deficiency, which is the key diagnostic clue.
Rises in parallel with PT; a very high INR with only mild bleeding suggests chronic liver disease rather than isolated vitamin K deficiency.
aPTT is often normal or only mildly prolonged because factor IX is less affected than factors II, VII and X; a normal aPTT does not exclude the diagnosis.
Platelets are normal in uncomplicated vitamin K deficiency; a low count suggests an alternative or coexisting cause such as DIC or liver disease.
Falls with the volume of blood lost; a normal hemoglobin early does not exclude significant bleeding.
Rises as the marrow responds to blood loss anemia.
Normal or high in vitamin K deficiency; a low fibrinogen points toward DIC or liver failure instead.
Elevated in infants with cholestasis or adults with biliary obstruction, the setting that causes malabsorption of vitamin K.
A conjugated (direct) predominance suggests cholestasis rather than hemolysis.
Elevated when the underlying cause is liver disease.
Markedly elevated in biliary obstruction and in infantile cholestasis.
Low in chronic liver disease or malabsorption.
Supports a cholestatic cause of fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption.
Low in malabsorption; a low B12 with prolonged PT suggests fat-soluble vitamin deficiency rather than an isolated clotting problem.

differential.name: Immune thrombocytopenia

differential.name: Liver failure with impaired clotting factor synthesis

differential.name: Warfarin or superwarfarin toxicity

differential.name: Child physical abuse

severity.mild: Minor oozing from the umbilical stump, circumcision site, or puncture sites with a few bruises; infant is well-appearing and feeding normally
severity.moderate: Visible bruising or active oozing from mucous membranes or the gastrointestinal tract; mild irritability or fussiness; hemoglobin falling
severity.severe: Significant gastrointestinal or mucosal bleeding with pallor, lethargy, or hemodynamic changes; possible early intracranial hemorrhage
severity.critical: Intracranial hemorrhage, exsanguinating bleeding, or shock; can be fatal or leave permanent neurologic injury

Significant blood loss or shock; resuscitate and transfuse as needed

red_flags.finding: Bleeding that continues after vitamin K administration
red_flags.meaning: Consider an alternative or coexisting cause such as DIC or liver failure

complications.name: Gastrointestinal hemorrhage
clues: Blood in the diaper or stool

complications.name: Iron deficiency anemia from chronic blood loss

special_populations.differences: Late vitamin K deficiency bleeding (2–12 weeks) occurs almost exclusively in exclusively breastfed infants, often with cholestasis, and can present with intracranial hemorrhage and no external bleeding.
Adults with cirrhosis may have prolonged PT from both vitamin K deficiency and impaired synthesis of clotting factors; bleeding may be less responsive to vitamin K alone.
Often presents with gastrointestinal bleeding or bruising on warfarin or after prolonged antibiotics, rather than umbilical or circumcision bleeding.

Vitamin K deficiency is uncommon in pregnancy but can occur with hyperemesis, malabsorption, or anticonvulsant use; newborns of mothers on enzyme-inducing anticonvulsants are at higher risk and should receive vitamin K prophylaxis.

key_questions.question: Did your baby receive a vitamin K shot at birth?
key_questions.looking_for: No vitamin K prophylaxis at birth strongly supports the diagnosis

key_questions.question: Is your baby exclusively breastfed, or are they getting formula or vitamin K supplementation?
key_questions.looking_for: Exclusive breastfeeding without supplementation is a major risk factor

key_questions.question: How old is your baby now?
key_questions.looking_for: First week of life (early) or 2–12 weeks (late) fits the classic timing

key_questions.question: Where is the bleeding coming from?
key_questions.looking_for: Umbilical stump, circumcision site, puncture sites, mucous membranes, or gastrointestinal tract

key_questions.question: Has your baby had any bruising without injury?
key_questions.looking_for: Spontaneous ecchymoses, especially in a pre-mobile infant

key_questions.question: Has your baby been more sleepy, fussy, or had any seizures or unusual movements?
key_questions.looking_for: Lethargy, poor feeding, or seizures suggesting intracranial hemorrhage

key_questions.question: Is your baby jaundiced, or have they had pale stools or dark urine?
For adults: do you have any condition that causes poor absorption, such as celiac disease, cystic fibrosis, or short bowel syndrome?
key_questions.looking_for: Chronic malabsorption as the underlying cause

key_questions.question: For adults: have you been on antibiotics for a long time, or are you taking warfarin?
key_questions.looking_for: Prolonged broad-spectrum antibiotics or warfarin use

key_questions.question: For adults: what does your diet look like? Do you eat leafy green vegetables?
key_questions.looking_for: Poor dietary vitamin K intake, especially with fat malabsorption

key_questions.question: Does anyone in the family have a bleeding disorder or bleed easily?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; a family history suggests an inherited coagulopathy

key_questions.question: Has there been any trauma, and does the bruising match the story?
key_questions.looking_for: Injury inconsistent with the mechanism or bruising in a pre-mobile infant raises concern for abuse

reasoning_points: Bleeding from the umbilical stump, circumcision site, puncture sites, or mucous membranes in a newborn, or easy bruising and mucosal bleeding in an adult with malabsorption
Risk factors: no vitamin K prophylaxis at birth, exclusive breastfeeding, cholestatic liver disease, chronic malabsorption, prolonged broad-spectrum antibiotics, or warfarin use
Prolonged PT and INR with a normal or only mildly prolonged aPTT and a normal platelet count
Correction of PT/INR within hours after parenteral vitamin K confirms vitamin K deficiency as the cause
Absence of petechiae, hemarthrosis, and deep muscle hematomas argues against platelet disorders and hemophilia
Look for and treat an underlying cause such as cholestasis, malabsorption, or biliary obstruction once the diagnosis is confirmed
Consider intracranial hemorrhage in any infant with seizures, lethargy, or a bulging fontanelle and image the head urgently

easy: Newborn in the first week of life who did not receive vitamin K prophylaxis
Bleeding from the umbilical stump or circumcision site
Prolonged PT/INR that corrects with vitamin K
Exclusively breastfed infant with no supplementation
medium: Late vitamin K deficiency bleeding at 2–12 weeks in an exclusively breastfed infant
Infant with jaundice and cholestasis causing fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption
Adult with celiac disease or cystic fibrosis presenting with bruising and prolonged PT
Normal aPTT with prolonged PT, which can be mistaken for liver disease alone
hard: Infant presenting with intracranial hemorrhage and no external bleeding
Adult on prolonged broad-spectrum antibiotics with mild oozing and a normal platelet count
Cirrhotic patient whose PT only partially corrects with vitamin K because of both deficiency and impaired synthesis
Bruising in a pre-mobile infant where physical abuse must be excluded
Warfarin or superwarfarin toxicity mimicking vitamin K deficiency
